headline: High-risk shared-runtime pair: OpenHands can read/write mounted files and use MCP, while oh-my-openagent injects MCP/hooks and broad egress, creating default pathways for leakage, conflict, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: oh-my-openagent uses runtime-injected MCPs and hooks, and OpenHands can use MCP servers and run browsers/subprocesses. That creates a plausible instruction-smuggling path if one agent’s outputs are fed into shared MCP or file channels. No direct shared channel is documented, so I avoid high.
conditions: IF both agents are connected to the same MCP server or hook chain
IF OpenHands ingests files or MCP outputs from oh-my-openagent as instructions
mitigations: Disable shared MCP servers between the two agents
Route inter-agent messages through a plain-text, human-reviewed queue
Add provenance tags to all MCP/tool outputs
Restrict hooks to read-only actions
requires-engineering: add parser hardening for instruction-like content

B_data_leakage.rationale: oh-my-openagent touches session history, project code, README.md, and provider auth data, while OpenHands reads and writes files in its runtime sandbox and can use broad network egress. If they share mounted files or credentials, sensitive content can flow from A into B and then out via B’s networked tools. The shared-volume path is plausible but not explicitly documented.
conditions: IF both agents mount the same workspace or cache directory
IF provider auth data or session history is present in files readable by OpenHands
mitigations: Separate workspaces and caches per agent
Remove secrets from any shared mount
Disable network egress for OpenHands during sensitive tasks
Rotate provider auth credentials after shared runs
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem ACLs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands can write the filesystem and modify git state, while oh-my-openagent has subprocess and browser execution plus per-installation session scope. If both operate on the same repo or mounted volume, concurrent writes and git mutations can collide and corrupt state. The overlap is directly supported by both profiles, so I rate this high.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository or mounted directory
IF OpenHands performs git operations while oh-my-openagent is editing files or spawning subprocesses
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories per agent
Serialize git writes with a lock file
Pause one agent before the other edits the repo
Use separate branches for each agent
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: oh-my-openagent can emit code/search results and OpenHands is an action-taking coding agent with shell and browser tools. If OpenHands treats A’s output as authoritative without verification, mistakes can cascade into edits, installs, or commits. The profiles support the pathway, but there is no direct evidence of blind trust, so medium fits.
conditions: IF OpenHands consumes oh-my-openagent output as task instructions or facts
IF no verification step is inserted before shell, package, or git actions
mitigations: Require a human review step before execution
Ask OpenHands to restate assumptions before acting
Compare outputs against source files or docs
Limit OpenHands to dry-run mode for first pass
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking gates

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source and docs-only, but oh-my-openagent handles provider auth prompts and session history while OpenHands handles model provider API keys and runtime-mounted files. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a low compliance gap is evident from retention/secret-handling differences.
conditions: IF the same regulated data is stored in both agents’ logs or mounted files
IF retention or deletion policies differ for session history versus runtime files
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared logs
Purge session history after each run
Keep API keys out of mounted workspaces
Document retention settings for both agents
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows
